clinicalPearls: An abnormally located parathyroid gland, most often reflecting embryological descent, found in sites such as the mediastinum, thymus, retro-oesophageal space, carotid sheath, or within the thyroid
Clinically important mainly as a cause of persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism when a hyperfunctioning ectopic gland is missed at the initial neck exploration

Superior glands, derived from the fourth pharyngeal pouch, tend to lie posteriorly or in a retro-oesophageal position, whereas inferior glands from the third pouch may descend with the thymus into the mediastinum
Biochemistry is that of primary hyperparathyroidism, with hypercalcaemia and inappropriately elevated PTH, but conventional imaging may fail to localise the culprit gland
Accurate preoperative localisation is essential and typically combines sestamibi scintigraphy with SPECT/CT and 4D-CT, supplemented by selective venous sampling in difficult cases
An intrathyroidal parathyroid can masquerade as a thyroid nodule and be overlooked unless specifically considered
Successful cure depends on targeted surgery guided by imaging and, where available, intraoperative PTH monitoring to confirm removal of all hyperfunctioning tissue
reference.pathophysiology: Ectopic parathyroid glands arise because the parathyroids migrate during embryogenesis: the superior glands develop from the fourth pharyngeal pouch and the inferior glands, together with the thymus, from the third pouch. Variations in this migration leave glands in unexpected positions, including retro-oesophageal and paraoesophageal tissue, the carotid sheath, within the thyroid, or descended into the anterior mediastinum with thymic tissue. When such a gland becomes an autonomously hyperfunctioning adenoma or hyperplastic gland, it produces primary hyperparathyroidism, but its aberrant location makes it difficult to find, and it is a frequent reason for failed neck exploration and persistent disease.
additionalDifferentials: Thyroid nodule mimicking an intrathyroidal parathyroid
Mediastinal mass such as thymoma or lymph node
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium and intact PTH confirming primary hyperparathyroidism
Sestamibi scintigraphy with SPECT/CT for functional localisation
4D-CT of the neck and mediastinum for anatomical localisation
Neck ultrasound including assessment for an intrathyroidal gland
Selective venous sampling for PTH when non-invasive imaging is discordant or negative
Intraoperative PTH monitoring to confirm complete excision
redFlags: Persistent or recurrent hypercalcaemia after apparently successful parathyroid surgery
Discordant or negative conventional imaging in confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism
A mediastinal lesion requiring more extensive surgical access
reference.prognosis: Once the ectopic hyperfunctioning gland is accurately localised and completely removed, hyperparathyroidism is usually cured; the main difficulty is localisation, and undetected glands lead to persistent disease and repeat surgery.
pitfalls: Terminating neck exploration without considering an ectopic mediastinal or retro-oesophageal gland
Missing an intrathyroidal parathyroid mistaken for a thyroid nodule
Relying on a single imaging modality when multimodal localisation is often required
Failing to use intraoperative PTH monitoring to confirm cure in reoperative cases
references: WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
management: Definitive treatment is precise preoperative localisation with sestamibi SPECT/CT, 4D-CT and, in difficult cases, selective venous sampling, followed by targeted surgical excision of the hyperfunctioning ectopic gland
Use intraoperative parathyroid hormone monitoring to confirm complete removal and biochemical cure
Plan a thoracic, minimally invasive or trans-sternal approach with the appropriate surgical team for mediastinal glands
Control significant hypercalcaemia before surgery with intravenous fluids and, where needed, cinacalcet or a bisphosphonate, and treat hypercalcaemic crisis
Where surgery is not feasible, manage hypercalcaemia long term with the calcimimetic cinacalcet and monitor renal and skeletal complications
Monitor postoperatively for hypocalcaemia, confirm cure and surveil for persistent or recurrent disease
Manage through an endocrine surgery multidisciplinary team and consider evaluation for familial hyperparathyroidism or multiple endocrine neoplasia
